Design,preparation,andcharacterizationofPNs/BS heterojunction

Amongthetwoillustrativeheterojunctioncomponentsselectedinthis study,specialfocusshouldbeplacedonthedesignandsynthesisof PNs.Asdistinctfrommostsemiconductormaterials(includingBiOI), phosphorenedemonstratesauniquelayer-dependentdirectbandgap accompanied by tunable redox capabilities of its charge carriers20. Thus, we initiate our study by employing density functional theory (DFT) calculations toinvestigate the bandgapenergy(E ) of PNs to g instruct the reasonable control over their layer thickness, thereby optimizingtheirperformanceasacomponentintheheterojunction. OurinvestigationrevealsthattheE valuesassociatedwithPNs,for g layersnumberingone,two,three,andfour,are1.70,1.48,0.93,and 0.66eV, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 1). This indicates that the controloverthelayernumberofPNsismorenecessarycomparedto BS.Giventhat,whileensuringthefullutilizationoftheentirevisible- light spectrum, a reduced number of layers in PNs can lead to enhancedredoxcapabilitiesofchargecarriers.Moreover,thesynth- esis of ultrathin PNs is expected to enhance their contact with BS, which is beneficial for strengthening the interfacial interaction betweenthetwocomponents.

Nevertheless,themostcommonlyusedliquidexfoliationmethod for PNs production frombulkblackphosphorus (BP) proves inade- quate in fulfilling this requirement, as multilayers are typically obtained (e.g., 5–8 phosphorene atomic layers using N-methyl-2- pyrrolidone(NMP),andeventhickerwithothersolvents)21–26.Thisis duetothesurfaceenergyofphosphorene(~58.6mJ/m2)ismismatched withthatofthewidelyemployedexfoliationsolvents,suchasNMP, acetone,ethanol,isopropanol(IPA),anddimethylformamide(DMF), hindering the enthalpy minimization of the mixed system27,28. How- ever, considering water’s significantly higher surface energy of ~102mJ/m2 and its miscibility with the aforementioned organic sol- vents, an organic-water mixture with an optimal surface energy for effectivePNsproductionisachievable.Thus,weinvestigatetheexfo- liationefficienciesof21distinctorganic-watermixturesforPNspro- duction employing the Lambert-Beer law as a fundamental analysis principle(SupplementaryFig.2).Asanticipated,weascertainadiverse range of mixtures exhibiting exceptional exfoliation performances, enabling the highly efficient generation of PNs. According to the experimentalresults,theoptimalsolventsareidentifiedasanethanol/ water system (V /V =50%) and a NMP/water system (V / ethanol water NMP V =80%).Giventhepotentialchallengeencounteredinremoving water NMPwithahighboilingpoint,theethanol/watersystemisselectedfor PNs production (see Supplementary Information for details of analysis).

Through the liquid exfoliation of bulk BP in the determined ethanol/water system, the outcome yields PNs characterized by a superior crystalline state, as validated by selected-area electron dif- fractionandRamanassessments(SupplementaryFig.3).Asdepicted inSupplementaryFig.4,theverticalextentdataextractedalongthe markedlinesrevealathicknessof~1.7–2.1nm,whichcorrespondsto 2–3atomiclayers,confirmingthesuccessfulproductionofultrathin PNs29.PNs/BSmaterialsarethenpreparedbyawetchemistrymethod, in which PNs are mixed with BS precursors (KI and Bi(NO) ·5H O), 3 2 enablingtheinsitugrowthofBSonPNs.Accordingtotheweightratios ofPNstoBS(xwt%),thesamplesaredenotedasxPNs/BS.Asshownin SupplementaryFig.5,theX-raydiffraction(XRD)patternof0.0PNs/BS clearlyindicatesitsalignmentwiththetetragonalphaseofBiOI(JCPDS No.10-0445).AcomparisonoftheXRDpatternsbetween0.0PNs/BS and0.8PNs/BSunderscoresthattheincorporationofPNshasaneg- ligibleimpactonthecrystallinestructureofBS.Moreover,itisnote- worthy that the XRD peaks associated with BP are conspicuously absentwithinthepatternof0.8PNs/BS.Thisabsenceisattributedto the fact that PNs are loaded at a relatively low concentration and exhibitaremarkabledegreeofdispersion.Thetransmissionelectron microscope(TEM)imageofPNsrevealsathin2Dflake-likestructure withwell-definededgesandsleekexternalsurfaces,whereastheTEM imageof0.0PNs/BSdisplaysa2Dsheet-likearchitecturemarkedby irregular edges and rough external surfaces (Fig. 1a, b). These 2D morphologicalfeaturesarefurthercorroboratedbyscanningelectron microscope(SEM)observations(SupplementaryFigs.6and 7).The high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) images of PNs and 0.0PNs/BS unveil their high crystalline quality (Supplementary Fig. 8). The image in Fig.1cillustratesaTEMviewof0.8PNs/BS,revealingthestackingofBS ontothesurfaceofultrathinPNs,establishinga“face-to-face”contact between the two 2D materials. The HRTEM image of 0.8PNs/BS demonstrateslatticefringesthatareconsistentwiththe(002)facetof BPandthe(110)facetofBiOI(Fig.1d)30,31.TheenergydispersiveX-ray spectroscopy(EDS)andX-rayphotoelectronspectroscopy(XPS)sur- veyresultsof0.8PNs/BSconcurwiththefindingsofTEMandHRTEM by confirming the elemental composition of Bi, O, I, and P in the material (Supplementary Fig. 9). The high-angle annular dark field- scanning transmission electron microscope (HAADF-STEM) image alongwiththecorrespondingelementalmappingimagesof0.8PNs/BS provideadditionalevidenceoftheconsistenthybridizationofPNsand BS in a uniform manner (Supplementary Fig. 10).Therefore, all the aforementionedresultsstronglyvalidatethesuccessfulpreparationof aheterojunctionofPNs/BS.

Stronginterfacialinteractionforimprovedchargecarrier transfer

The observed “face to face” contact between the two 2D compo- nents,PNsandBS,withintheconstructedheterojunction,isantici- patedtocreateastronginterfacialinteractionbetweenthelayers.To confirm this, synchrotron-based X-ray absorption near-edge struc- ture(XANES)analysisisemployed.TheBiL -edgeabsorptionedge 3 position of 0.8PNs/BS shows a negative shift compared to that of 0.0PNs/BS,suggestingtheoccurrenceofelectrontransferfromPNs to BS within the heterojunction (Fig. 2a). To further validate the electron transfer between the two materials, DFT calculations are performed. Figure 2b shows the differential charge density of the compositesystem,withblueandyellowregionsrepresentingcharge depletionandaccumulation,respectively.Theresultindicatesthat the surface of BS attracts electrons from neighboring PNs. Such electrontransferbehaviorisoftenassociatedwiththeestablishment ofanintimateelectronicinteractionbetweendistinctheterojunction moieties. To rationalize this observation, the work function (Φ) valuesofthetwocomponentsarecalculated,resultingin4.61eVfor phosphoreneand5.89eVforBiOI(Fig.2c,d).ThedisparityinΦ,in theory,canpromoteadirectionalelectrontransferbetweenPNsand BS,therebyestablishinganinternalelectricfieldthatinducesinter- layerelectroniccoupling.Moreimportantly,suchastronginterfacial electronicinteractionisexpectedtofacilitateafastchargetransfer processbetweenthetwomaterials.

Buildingonthisexpectation,femtosecondtransientabsorption spectroscopy is carried out. As illustrated inFig. 2e, f, excitation at 350nm induces distinct positive peaks for both 0.0PNs/BS and 0.8PNs/BSinthetimescaleof0.5–200ps,indicatingthedominanceof excited-state absorption during this interval. In contrast, the time range of 500ps–3ns ischaracterized by prominent negative peaks, demonstratingthatthegradualrelaxationofexcited-statepopulation backtogroundstateovertime.Interestingly,for0.8PNs/BS,inaddi- tiontoaground-statebleachingpeakat~526nm,astrongernegative featureisevidentonthelongerwavelengthside.Thiscanbeattributed to the stimulated emission resulting from the electron-hole recombinationbetweenPNsandBS.Figure2gillustratesthenormal- ized recovery kinetics of 0.0PNs/BS at 520nm (fitted using a two- exponential function), reflecting the interband diffusion and the trappingbyshallowtrapstatesofphoto-inducedelectrons.Theinte- gration of PNs with BSgives riseto anadditional ultrafastpathway (~2.1ps), which can be attributed to the transfer of photo-induced electronsbetweenthetwocomponents(Fig.2h).Thisultrafasttransfer processisanticipatedtomitigatetherecombinationofelectronsand holes occurring within each individual component, effectively pre- ventingphotonenergylossfromakineticperspective.

To validate this, the charge carrier separation efficiencies of 0.0PNs/BS and 0.8PNs/BS are systematically investigated using a range of characterization techniques. First, transient photo-current (TPC) response measurement is conducted. As depicted in Supple- mentary Fig. 12a, the TPC response of 0.8PNs/BS, which is sig- nificantly higher than that of 0.0PNs/BS, suggests an improved efficiency in the separation of electron-hole pairs upon the incor- poration of PNs with BS. Additionally, the results from electro- chemicalimpedancespectroscopy(EIS)measurementdemonstratea smallersemicircleradiusintheNyquistplotof0.8PNs/BScompared withthatof0.0PNs/BS,implyingareducedchargetransferresistance for 0.8PNs/BS, thereby promoting more efficient charge carrier separation(SupplementaryFig.12b).Furthermore,thesteady-state photoluminescence(PL)resultsofthesamplesrevealareducedPL intensityfor0.8PNs/BSincontrastto0.0PNs/BS,suggestingasup- pressedchargecarrierrecombinationin0.8PNs/BS(Supplementary Fig.12c).Moreover,thetransient-statePLresultsshowninSupple- mentary Fig. 12d exhibit an increase in average PL lifetime, from 19.8nsfor0.0PNs/BSto23.9nsfor0.8PNs/BS.Thisfurthersupports the higher electron-hole separation efficiency of 0.8PNs/BS, in agreementwiththeTPC,EIS,andsteady-statePLresults.Hence,all theabove-mentionedexperimentalfindingscollectivelyvalidatethat the energy loss during charge transfer process is effectively mitigated.

BoostedredoxcapacityforelevatedROSproduction

Theseparatedphoto-inducedchargecarrierscansubsequentlyparti- cipate in catalytic redox reactions for ROS generation. The redox capacitiesofthesechargecarriersaredeterminedbythebandalign- menttypeoftheheterojunction,which,inturn,governstheenergy efficiency of the ensuing ROS generation process.Considering this, band-structure characterizations are performed for the two hetero- junctioncomponents.First,theE ofBSisderivedfromtheplotof g (αhν)nversushνshowninSupplementaryFig.13a,whereαrepresents absorption coefficient, h stands for Planck constant, and ν denotes lightfrequency32.Inthisequation,nissetto1/2duetotheindirect bandgapnatureofBS.Consequently,thedeterminedE valueofBS g standsat1.68eV.Subsequenttothis,XPSvalence-bandspectroscopy analysisisconductedforBS.AsillustratedinSupplementaryFig.13b, thevalence-bandvalueofBSisobservedtobe1.36VversusNHE.This leadstothecalculationoftheconduction-bandvalueofBS,whichis foundtobe−0.32VversusNHE(SupplementaryTable1).Furthermore, theE ofPNsisascertainedthroughUV–visible(UV–vis)absorption g spectroscopyanalysis.AsshowninSupplementaryFig.13c,theiden- tifiedabsorptionedgeofPNsat731nmcorrespondstoanE valueof g 1.70eV. We then execute a Mott-Schottky test, revealing the n-type semiconductorcharacteristicofPNs(SupplementaryFig.13d).Thus, theflat-bandpotentialofPNs,extractedfromtheMott-Schottkyresult, canofferaroughestimationfortheconduction-bandvalue.Conse- quently,theconduction-bandvalueofPNsisestablishedat−0.44V versusNHE,andthevalence-bandvalueisthencalculatedtobe1.26V versusNHE(SupplementaryTable1).

Combining the band structures of PNs and BS with the above experimental and DFT findings on the electron transfer direction betweenthem,atypicalS-schemebandalignmentisexpectedatthe PNs/BSinterface(Fig.3a–c).Inthisbandalignment,PNs,characterized byamorenegativeconduction-bandposition,actasthereduction- typecomponent,whileBS,withamorepositivevalence-bandposition, function as the oxidation-type component. In the absence of light irradiation, electrons spontaneouslytransfer fromPNs to BS,estab- lishing an internal electric field across the heterojunction directed fromPNstoBS.Underlightirradiation,thisbuilt-infieldfacilitatesthe recombinationofphoto-excitedelectronsintheconductionbandof BS with photo-induced holes in the valence band of PNs. Conse- quently,energeticallyfavorablechargecarriersarepreservedinthe conductionbandofPNsandthevalencebandofBS.SuchanS-scheme bandalignmentisanticipatedtoaugmenttheROS-productionabilities of charge carriers, effectivelymitigating photon energy lossfroma thermodynamicperspective.

To confirm this,the visible-light-induced ROS generation ofthe samples is evaluated using specific reactions involving probe mole- cules. Specifically, nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) can react with (cid:129)O−, 2 leading to a reduction in the absorption intensity at 259nm. As depicted in Fig. 3d, 0.8PNs/BS demonstrates the highest NBT con- sumptionamongthetestedsamples,correspondingtoa(cid:129)O−steady- 2 stateconcentrationof4.90×10−9Minitsreactionsystem,significantly surpassing the concentration observed in 0.0PNs/BS system (1.25×10−9M).Furthermore,furfurylalcohol(FFA),awidelyacknowl- edgedprobefor1O generation,ismonitoredforitsdecaytoquanti- 2 tativelyassessthe1O-generationactivitiesofthesamples(Fig.3e).The 2 1O steady-stateconcentrationin0.8PNs/BSsystemisdeterminedtobe 2 2.02 ×10−13M,exceedingthecorrespondingvaluein0.0PNs/BSsystem (1.38×10−13M). Moreover, p-chlorobenzoic acid (pCBA) is used as a reactiveagenttoevaluatethe(cid:129)OH-generationabilitiesofthematerials. As shown in Fig. 3f, 0.8PNs/BS exhibits the highest (cid:129)OH-production capacity, as evidenced by its more rapid pCBA decomposition com- paredtotheothertestedsamples.Thecorresponding(cid:129)OHsteady-state concentrationisdeterminedtobe5.20×10−14M,surpassingthevalue observedin0.0PNs/BSsystem(2.17×10−14M).Theresultsofelectron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy further support these findings, offeringadditionalevidenceoftheenhancedgenerationactivitiesof (cid:129)O−,1O,and(cid:129)OHover0.8PNs/BSrelativeto0.0PNs/BS(Supplemen- 2 2 taryFig.14).WethenexaminetheH O-productioncapacitiesofthe 2 2 samplesusingiodometricanalysis(Fig.3g).After60minofreaction, the accumulated HO concentrations in 0.0PNs/BS and 0.8PNs/BS 2 2 systemsarequantifiedtobe3.3and6.6μM,respectively,indicatingthe superior HO production activity of 0.8PNs/BS. Collectively, these 2 2- experimentalfindingsunequivocallyconfirmtheeffectivemitigationof energylossduringROSgenerationprocess.

Visible-lightphotocatalyticwaterdisinfectionperformance

An assessment of the photocatalytic disinfection activities of the samplesisthencarriedout.Gram-negativebacteriumE.coli,withan initial concentration of 7log, is used as a process indicator in all experimentsunlessotherwiseindicated.Visiblelightwithanoptical power density of ~100mW cm−2 isgeneratedusingasolarsimulator.As depictedinSupplementaryFig.15,PNsdemonstrateaminimalpho- tocatalyticdisinfectioneffectagainstE.coli,withbacterialconcentra- tion decreasing by less than 1log after 60min of illumination. Nonetheless, their incorporation markedly improves the photo- catalytic antibacterial performance of BS across varying loading amounts (Fig. 4a). Notably, 0.8PNs/BS shows the highest photo- catalyticwaterdisinfectionperformance,achievingacomplete7-log inactivation of E. coli (> 99.99999% disinfection efficiency) in only 5min of visible-light irradiation. In contrast, control experiments conducted under solely visible-light exposure or inthe presence of 0.8PNs/BS under a dark condition result in disinfection efficiencies below0.25logafter120min,demonstratingthatbacterialinactivation isattributedtovisible-lightphotocatalysis(0.8PNs/BScanharvestthe entire visible-light spectrum, as evidenced by UV–vis diffuse reflec- tance spectroscopy) (Supplementary Fig. 16). The contributions of variousROSduringthedisinfectionprocessofE.coliareinvestigated through a scavenger study. The experimental results illustrated in SupplementaryFig.17indicatetheparticipationoffourdistinctROS forbacterialinactivation,withcontributionsof(cid:129)O −>1O >H O >(cid:129)OH. 2 2 2 2 TheseROScontributetoE.coliinactivationbydisruptingcellmem- brane permeability, inhibiting energy metabolism, and damaging intracellularcomponents(SupplementaryFig.18).Themechanismof photocatalytic water disinfection by 0.8PNs/BS is shown in Supple- mentary Fig. 19. The broad-spectrum photocatalytic antibacterial activityof0.8PNs/BSisthendemonstratedbyitseffectivedisinfection of other waterborne bacteria, including E.faecalis,S.aureus,and P. aeruginosa(SupplementaryFig.20).Notably,theapproachproposed inthisstudy,whichstrategicallyoptimizesthecompatibilitybetween the macroscopic geometric architecture and microscopic band structureofheterojunctioncomponents,exhibitsbroadapplicability, asevidencedbythesignificantlyenhancedphotocatalyticantibacterial activitiesobservedupontheintegrationofPNswithBiOBrorBiOCl nanosheets(SupplementaryFigs.21and 22).

Thephotocatalyticantibacterialperformanceof0.8PNs/BS,witha 7-loginactivationofE.coliwithin5minundervisible-lightillumination, isconsideredoneofthemostremarkablebasedonathoroughreview oftheexistingliterature,particularlyintermsoftheextentofthelog reductioninbacterialconcentrationandtherapidityofdisinfection process(Fig.4bandSupplementaryTable2).Comparedwiththose thatachieveacompleteinactivationofE.coliwithin30min,suchas (Al O @v-MoS )/Cu,Cu-MoS ,andF-g-C N -30-EP,thebacterialcon- 2 3 2 2 3 4 centrationreductionachievedby0.8PNs/BSsurpassesthemby1-2log. Asfordisinfectionsystemscontaininganinitialbacterialconcentra- tionof7log,thereportedantimicrobialmaterialsthusfarnecessitatea minimumof60mintoachievethetotalinactivationofE.coli,whereas thesematerials,suchasSGO-ZnO-Ag,areaccompaniedbyacertain degree of biological intolerance. To the best of our knowledge, no previously reported photocatalysts have demonstrated such an extraordinarydisinfectionefficacywhenconfrontedwithaninitialE. coliconcentrationof7log.

Moreover, the photocatalytic water disinfection efficacy of 0.8PNs/BS is compared with that of the widely-studied P25 TiO 2 (20nm).AsshowninFig.4c,0.8PNs/BSoutperformsP25TiO under 2 real-sunlight irradiation (10:00 AM, local time, September 6, 2023, NortheastNormalUniversity,43.83°N,125.43°E),achievingacomplete inactivationof7logofE.coliinonly45s.Thiscorrespondstoafirst- orderdisinfectionrate(k)of9.30min−1(R2=0.97),whichexceedsthat ofP25TiO (k=0.042min−1,R2=0.95)byapproximately221-fold.More 2 importantly,0.8PNs/BSdemonstratesitsapplicabilityinacontinuous- flow fixed-bed reactor, enabling water purification for up to 24h, underscoringitspromiseforpracticalPOUwaterdisinfectionappli- cations(Fig.4d).

In conclusion, by utilizing PNs and BS as model materials, we demonstratethatoptimizingthecompatibilitybetweenthemacro- scopic geometric architecture and microscopic band structure of heterojunction components can effectively overcome both the kinetic and thermodynamic limitations of photo-induced charge carriers. Experimental findings, supported by DFT calculations, revealastronginterfacialinteractionbetweenthetwocomponents, enablinganultrafastelectrontransferprocess(~2.1ps).Furthermore, the established S-scheme band alignment promotes the efficient accumulation of electrons and holes with enhanced redox cap- abilities. Consequently, the energy from visible spectrum is effec- tively utilized for bacterial inactivation. Under real sunlight, the synthesized 0.8PNs/BS exhibits a subminute photocatalytic water disinfectionability,achievingacompleteinactivationof7-logE.coli within 45s. This delivers E. coli inactivation ~221 times faster than commercialP25TiO .Additionally,incorporating0.8PNs/BSintoa 2 continuous-flowfixed-bedreactorallowsforsustainablewaterpur- ification for up to 24h, underscoring its suitability for practical POUwaterdisinfection.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have attempted to optimize the compatibility between the macroscopic geometric and microscopic band structures of the heterojunction components to address the kinetic and thermodynamic limitations of photo-induced charge carriers. However, several critical issues remain unresolved. The resulting materials do not exhibit a well-ordered structure, and electron microscopy images fail to reveal any remarkable or novel features. Furthermore, the performance data presented do not demonstrate any significant improvement over previously reported results, raising concerns about the novelty and impact of the work. Given these limitations, I am unable to recommend this manuscript for publication in its current form. The work may be more suitable for submission to a more specialized journal rather than a broad scientific journal like Nature Communications.

Responses to thecomments and suggestions are listed below.
Reviewer#1
Comments: The authors have attempted to optimize the compatibility between the
macroscopic geometric and microscopic band structures of the heterojunction
components to address the kinetic and thermodynamic limitations of photo-induced
charge carriers. However, several critical issues remain unresolved. The resulting
materials do not exhibit a well-ordered structure, and electron microscopyimages failto reveal anyremarkableor novel features. Furthermore, the performance data
presented do not demonstrate any significant improvement over previously reported
results, raising concerns about the noveltyandimpact ofthe work. Given these
limitations, I am unable to recommend this manuscript for publication in its current
form. The work may be more suitable for submission to a more specialized journal
rather thanabroadscientificjournallikeNatureCommunications.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the rigorous and thoughtful
comments. We fully understand your concerns regarding the structural order of the
material and its disinfection performance. After several months of careful
consideration and revision, we have provided detailed clarifications on these two
aspects below. If our efforts still fall short of your expectations, we would be deeply
grateful for more specific guidance, which would allow us to further improve and
refine themanuscript withyour valuable assistance.
1. Regarding “The resulting materials do not exhibit a well-ordered structure, and
electron microscopyimages failto reveal anyremarkableor novel features”.
Response: In response to the reviewer’s comment on the absence of a
well-ordered structure in the TEM images, we provide the following clarification.
Indeed, electron microscopy images of many heterojunction systems often reveal a
certain degree of ordering, particularly in 0D/2D or 0D/3D composite materials. This
is largely attributable to the small size and distinct morphological feature of the 0D
components, which offer strong contrast and clear geometric distinction when
dispersed on 2D or 3D substrates.As a result, such composites tend to exhibit visually
recognizable ordering. For example, the 0D/3D composite reported in Nature
Communications (2024, 15: 4807) clearly illustrates this phenomenon:
[Figure Redacted]
FigureR1.ElectronmicroscopyimagesofIn O /Nb O heterojunctionillustratingthedeposition
2 3 2 5
of0Dmaterialsontoa3Dsubstrate.
However, the observation of well-defined ordering in 2D/2D heterostructures
remains a well-known and intrinsicchallenge, not specific to our system. In our study,
both PNs and BS possess characteristic 2D features and exhibit comparable lateral
dimensions. The inherently limited morphological contrast between the two
components makes it intrinsically difficult to resolve ordered interfaces at the
nanoscale. More importantly, physical perturbations during material preparation
further compromise structural ordering. For instance, the ultrasonic exfoliation
process for PNs production inevitably leads to fragmentation and edge irregularities;
and during the assembly of PNs and BS, random stacking orientations—such as
displacement, twisting, and slight curling of nanosheets—are essentially unavoidable.
These factors collectively diminish the likelihood of obtaining a well-ordered
compositestructure.
Recently, we have extensively surveyed the literature, including numerous
representative studies on 2D/2D heterojunctions. It is found that similar structural
features are widely reported across the field: even in seminal works, electron
microscopy images typically show coexisting nanosheets without consistent stacking
orientations and rarely display pronounced long-range ordering. For example, the
2D/2D composite reported in Journal of the American Chemical Society (2017, 139:
13234-13242) illustrates nanosheets with irregular orientations and no apparent
long-range order:
[Figure Redacted]
FigureR2.TEMimageof2D/2Dg-C N /BP.

illustrates similar randomly oriented nanosheets:

Hence, we believe our structural characterizations are consistent with what can
reasonably beexpected from this class ofmaterials.
Nonetheless, this comment prompts us to further strengthen our experimental
evidence. We have added SEM images to characterize the morphology of each
components individually, clearly demonstrating that both PNs and BS exhibit
well-defined 2D structures in their monomeric states, particularly with identifiable
ordering. While, as discussed above, the ordered nature of the final 2D/2D composite
cannot be guaranteed, this does not detract from the key claim of our paper that “PNs
and BS are compatible in terms of their macroscopic geometric structures”.
Additionally,TEM analysis of the composite reveals interfacial stacking between PNs
and BS, and the elemental mappings indicate a high degree of spatial co-localization,
further supporting the assertion of our paper that “PNs and BS form intimate
“face-to-face” contacts”. We hope that this clarification and the newly included data
adequately address thisconcern.

perspective” is examined in terms of what thermodynamic point of view and

Response: We thank the reviewer for the comment. From a thermodynamic
perspective, the generation of ROS during photocatalysis is governed by the redox
potentials of the relevant reactions relative to the semiconductor’s conduction and
valence band edges. If the conduction band minimum or valence band maximum of
the photocatalyst does not possess sufficient potential to drive the desired redox
reactions, the formation of ROS is thermodynamically limited, leading to energy loss.
As you noted, the relevant thermodynamic parameters essentially correspond to
whether the semiconductor’s conduction and valence band edges are sufficiently
positioned to drive the desired redox reactions. In response, we have supplemented

42.What does theaccumulation oflines in Figure2.(e),(f) indicate?
Response: Thanks for the comment. The data of Figure 2e and f can probe the
ultrafast dynamics of photo-excited charge carriers in 0.8PNs/BS system. By
monitoring ΔA over timescales from 0.5 ps to 3 ns, this technique allows us to
distinguish different processes: early-time positive signals reflect excited-state
absorption and carrier generation, while later-time negative signals correspond to
ground-state bleaching and stimulated emission, revealing carrier relaxation and
recombination. Importantly, the comparison between 0.0PNs/BS and 0.8PNs/BS
demonstrates enhanced stimulated emission in the latter, indicating more efficient
charge transfer across the heterojunction. Therefore, these data provide direct
evidence of how the heterojunction affects charge separation and recombination
dynamics, which is crucial for understanding and optimizingphotocatalyticactivity.

recombining radiatively. The connection arises because faster carrier separation

52.Does thetype ofBS affect planS-scheme?
Response: Thanks for the comment. The construction of an S-scheme
heterojunction mainly relies on two prerequisites: (i) the two semiconductors should
possess appropriate band structures to achieve staggered alignment, and (ii) there
should be a sufficiently large Fermi level difference to drive the internal electric field
for directional charge transfer (Chem, 2020, 6, 1543-1559). These two aspects are the
decisive factors for establishing an S-scheme charge transfer pathway. Whether BS is
p-type or n-type does not play the primary role. In practice, even n-n or p-p
combinations can form an effective S-scheme charge transfer pathway, provided the
above two conditions are met.Therefore, the type of BS is not the dominant factor; its
band edge positionsandFermi level alignment with PNsare thekey determinants.

58. What is your reason for writing this sentence “In this band alignment, PNs,
characterized by a more negative conduction-band position, act as the reduction-type
component, while BS, with a more positive valence-band position, function as the
oxidation-type component”.
Response: Thanks for the comment. The terminology of “reduction-type
component” and “oxidation-type component” reflects the distinct energetic positions
of the two semiconductors and the functional roles of their surviving charge carriers
under illumination. Specifically, PNs possess a more negative conduction-band
position, so the photo-excited electrons that remain in the conduction band after
interfacial recombination exhibit strong reduction potential. Conversely, BS have a
more positive valence-band position, and the photo-induced holes preserved in its
valence band show strong oxidation capability. This reduction–oxidation
complementarity is central to the S-scheme mechanism: the internal electric field
drives the recombination of low-energy carriers (electrons in BS and holes in PNs),
while selectively retaining the high-energy electrons in PNs and high-energy holes in
BS. As a result, the heterostructure maximizes the utilization of the intrinsic strong
redox potentials of the two components. The rationale for writing the sentence you
mentioned is now directly connected to the subsequent explanation in our manuscript.
Pleasesee pages 13-14 lines 258-266 in therevised manuscript as follows:
In the absence of light irradiation, electrons spontaneously transfer from PNs to BS,
establishing an internal electric field across the heterojunction directed from PNs to
BS. Under light irradiation, this built-in field facilitates the recombination of
photo-excited electrons in the conduction band of BS with photo-induced holes in the
valence band of PNs. Consequently, energetically favorable charge carriers are
preserved in the conduction band of PNs and the valence band of BS. Such an
S-scheme band alignment is anticipated to augment the ROS-production abilities of
charge carriers, effectively mitigating photon energy loss from a thermodynamic
perspective.
59.Are synthesized samples reusable (Recycling performance)? Please Perform XRD
analysis even after recovery (reuse).
Response: Thanks for the comment. We would like to emphasize an important
consideration regarding the evaluation of catalyst reusability. While many previous
studies, including some of our own prior works, relay on repeated batch experiments
to assess material recyclability, this approach has inherent limitations. Firstly, the
separation of photocatalyst powders from bacterial cells or bacterial residues is
technically challenging and often incomplete, which can lead to misleading
conclusions about material stability. Secondly,during repeated use,inevitable material
loss may occur, leading to a decrease in the actual recovery yield and affecting the
accuracy of performance evaluation. More importantly, powdered photocatalysts are
primarily research tools used to elucidate fundamental mechanisms, but are not
practical for real-world water disinfection applications. Therefore, evaluating material
stabilitysolely based onrepeated batch recycling tests lacks practical relevance.
To address this, we have pioneered the incorporation of our catalyst into a
continuous-flow fixed-bed reactor, enabling the direct assessment of disinfection
performance stability over extended operation (Advanced Materials. 2025, 37,
2410221). In the current work, our results demonstrate that after 24 h of continuous
operation, the disinfection efficiency remains above 99.99%, confirming the excellent
reusability ofthecatalyst ina realisticapplication setting.

27. In comment 33, do other parameters such as solvent viscosity and polarity also
have an effect?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. Indeed, other solvent
parameters can also influence the exfoliation process. Taking polarity, as you
mentioned, as an example, it can affect the interactions between 2D materials and
exfoliating mediums. As described in Science, 2011, 331: 568-571, the Hansen
solubility parameters provide an approach to quantify how exfoliating medium
influences the exfoliation process. These parameters incorporate three contributions to
the cohesive energy density: dispersion, polar, and hydrogen-bonding interactions. In
practice, effective exfoliation of a specific 2D material can only be achieved when all
three parameters (dispersion, polar, and hydrogen bond) of the solvent closely match
those of the 2D material. As can be seen, polarity is not an independent parameter,
rather, it is inherently embedded within the Hansen parameter set. That is to say,
although polarity is one of the parameters influencing exfoliation, its effect cannot be
clearly isolated from other intermolecular interactions, making it methodologically
challenging to use polarity as an independent screening criterion. In other words,
while polarity does play a role, it is not appropriate to treat it as a standalone indicator
for solvent selection.
In contrast, the surface energy is an independent parameter that has been widely
and successfully used for initial solvent selection. Although other parameters may
influence the exfoliation process, their existence does not undermine the validity of
using surface energy as a reliable descriptor, which is well supported by the
experimental results in this work. Also, many classical studies have employed surface
energy as a guiding parameter to identify suitable exfoliating mediums for various 2D
materials (J. Am. Chem. Soc, 2013, 135: 18-21; ACS Nano, 2016, 10: 2745-2751; Nat.
Nanotechnol, 2008, 3: 563-568). We hope that this clarification addresses your
concern.

For semiconductor heterojunctions, the key photophysical processes following
light excitation include excited-state absorption, ground-state bleaching, and
stimulated emission. It is worth noting that while all these processes can occur, they
evolve on different time scales. To facilitate understanding, we give an example: upon
light excitation, a molecule can undergo numerous distinct photophysical processes
(such as fluorescence, phosphorescence, internal conversion, and so on), as depicted
in the following schematic:
23
[Figure Redacted]
All these processes may take place within a photo-excited system, but their
characteristic lifetimes differ by several orders of magnitude, ranging from fs-s, as
shown below:
[Figure Redacted]
Similarly, after light excitation, in semiconductor heterojunctions, processes such
as excited-state absorption, ground-state bleaching, and stimulated emission also take
place on different time scales. To investigate these ultrafast photophysical processes,
femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy, conducted in our study, is a
powerful technique, as it allows direct tracking of the dynamic evolution of
these processes. The configuration of a femtosecond transient absorption
spectrometer is illustrated as follows:
[Figure Redacted]
In the above figure, the light emitted from the green instrument is used to excite
the sample, and after a very short delay (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......), a probe beam (from the
blue instrument) monitors the changes in the sample’s absorption. Femtosecond
transient absorption spectroscopy can be understood as an “ultrafast version” of
UV-vis absorption spectroscopy, recording the evolution of the sample’s absorption
over time with femtosecond time resolution. However, when directly comparing
absorption spectra at, for example, 0.0 ps and 0.5 ps, it is difficult to visually discern
significant differences, as the changes are typically very small. To facilitate
observation, the data in femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy are plotted
using ΔA on the vertical axis, where ΔA = A − A , representing the difference
excited ground
between the excited-state and ground-state absorption. The sign of ΔA can be used to
identify which photophysical process dominates at a given timescale. For instance,
when ΔA < 0, this indicates the occurrence of ground-state bleaching. This is because
that, before excitation, most electrons in the semiconductor material reside in the
ground state. Upon light excitation, some of these electrons are promoted to the
excited state, reducing the population of ground-state electrons—that is, fewer
electrons are available to absorb the probe beam (from the blue instrument). As a
result, the measured absorption signal decreases, manifesting as a negative ΔA.
In summary, based on the detailed explanation above, we hope it is now clear
what the curves in Figures 2e and f represent: each curve corresponds to the
absorption change between the excited-state and ground-state sample (0.0PNs/BS or
0.8PNs/BS) at a specific delay time (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......). Plotting the curves measured
at different delay times on one figure is simply a way to visually illustrate the spectral
evolution over time (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......), and does not imply any “accumulation” of
the signal. We hope this explanation makes it clear.

In more detail, for example, in the case of O reduction to H O , the
2 2 2

conduction-band potential of a semiconductor and the redox potential of this reaction

2 2 2

Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. To carefully explain

selected a schematic illustration from a key literature (Nat. Commun, 2024, 15: 4807),
as shown below:
[Figure Redacted]
Figure R3. Schematic illustration of the charge transfer mechanism in an S-type heterojunction.
In this figure, the band structure of a typical S-scheme heterojunction is depicted.
The light blue arrow indicates the direction of the internal electric field. The electric
field points from the positively charged region to the negatively charged region.
Under this field, electrons (negatively charged) experience a force opposite to the
11
field direction, while holes (positively charged) are driven along the field direction.
As a result, the electric field facilitates the recombination of photo-excited electrons
in the conduction band of the left-hand component with photo-induced holes in the
valence band of the right-hand component. As a result, photo-generated charge
carriers with strong redox capabilities in the conduction band of the right-hand
component and the valence band of the left-hand component are preserved, thereby
enabling the so-called “efficient electron and hole separation.” This mechanism is
consistent with previously reported studies (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. Engl, 2020, 59:
5218-5225; Chem, 2020, 6: 1543-1559). We hope this explanation addresses your
question.

27. In comment 33, do other parameters such as solvent viscosity and polarity also
have an effect?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. Indeed, other solvent
parameters can also influence the exfoliation process. Taking polarity, as you
mentioned, as an example, it can affect the interactions between 2D materials and
exfoliating mediums. As described in Science, 2011, 331: 568-571, the Hansen
solubility parameters provide an approach to quantify how exfoliating medium
influences the exfoliation process. These parameters incorporate three contributions to
the cohesive energy density: dispersion, polar, and hydrogen-bonding interactions. In
practice, effective exfoliation of a specific 2D material can only be achieved when all
three parameters (dispersion, polar, and hydrogen bond) of the solvent closely match
those of the 2D material. As can be seen, polarity is not an independent parameter,
rather, it is inherently embedded within the Hansen parameter set. That is to say,
although polarity is one of the parameters influencing exfoliation, its effect cannot be
clearly isolated from other intermolecular interactions, making it methodologically
challenging to use polarity as an independent screening criterion. In other words,
while polarity does play a role, it is not appropriate to treat it as a standalone indicator
for solvent selection.
In contrast, the surface energy is an independent parameter that has been widely
and successfully used for initial solvent selection. Although other parameters may
influence the exfoliation process, their existence does not undermine the validity of
using surface energy as a reliable descriptor, which is well supported by the
experimental results in this work. Also, many classical studies have employed surface
energy as a guiding parameter to identify suitable exfoliating mediums for various 2D
materials (J. Am. Chem. Soc, 2013, 135: 18-21; ACS Nano, 2016, 10: 2745-2751; Nat.
Nanotechnol, 2008, 3: 563-568). We hope that this clarification addresses your
concern.

For semiconductor heterojunctions, the key photophysical processes following
light excitation include excited-state absorption, ground-state bleaching, and
stimulated emission. It is worth noting that while all these processes can occur, they
evolve on different time scales. To facilitate understanding, we give an example: upon
light excitation, a molecule can undergo numerous distinct photophysical processes
(such as fluorescence, phosphorescence, internal conversion, and so on), as depicted
in the following schematic:
23
[Figure Redacted]
All these processes may take place within a photo-excited system, but their
characteristic lifetimes differ by several orders of magnitude, ranging from fs-s, as
shown below:
[Figure Redacted]
Similarly, after light excitation, in semiconductor heterojunctions, processes such
as excited-state absorption, ground-state bleaching, and stimulated emission also take
place on different time scales. To investigate these ultrafast photophysical processes,
femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy, conducted in our study, is a
powerful technique, as it allows direct tracking of the dynamic evolution of
these processes. The configuration of a femtosecond transient absorption
spectrometer is illustrated as follows:
[Figure Redacted]
In the above figure, the light emitted from the green instrument is used to excite
the sample, and after a very short delay (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......), a probe beam (from the
blue instrument) monitors the changes in the sample’s absorption. Femtosecond
transient absorption spectroscopy can be understood as an “ultrafast version” of
UV-vis absorption spectroscopy, recording the evolution of the sample’s absorption
over time with femtosecond time resolution. However, when directly comparing
absorption spectra at, for example, 0.0 ps and 0.5 ps, it is difficult to visually discern
significant differences, as the changes are typically very small. To facilitate
observation, the data in femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy are plotted
using ΔA on the vertical axis, where ΔA = A − A , representing the difference
excited ground
between the excited-state and ground-state absorption. The sign of ΔA can be used to
identify which photophysical process dominates at a given timescale. For instance,
when ΔA < 0, this indicates the occurrence of ground-state bleaching. This is because
that, before excitation, most electrons in the semiconductor material reside in the
ground state. Upon light excitation, some of these electrons are promoted to the
excited state, reducing the population of ground-state electrons—that is, fewer
electrons are available to absorb the probe beam (from the blue instrument). As a
result, the measured absorption signal decreases, manifesting as a negative ΔA.
In summary, based on the detailed explanation above, we hope it is now clear
what the curves in Figures 2e and f represent: each curve corresponds to the
absorption change between the excited-state and ground-state sample (0.0PNs/BS or
0.8PNs/BS) at a specific delay time (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......). Plotting the curves measured
at different delay times on one figure is simply a way to visually illustrate the spectral
evolution over time (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......), and does not imply any “accumulation” of
the signal. We hope this explanation makes it clear.

Response: In response to the reviewer’s comment on the absence of a
well-ordered structure in the TEM images, we provide the following clarification.
Indeed, electron microscopy images of many heterojunction systems often reveal a
certain degree of ordering, particularly in 0D/2D or 0D/3D composite materials. This
is largely attributable to the small size and distinct morphological feature of the 0D
components, which offer strong contrast and clear geometric distinction when
dispersed on 2D or 3D substrates.As a result, such composites tend to exhibit visually
recognizable ordering. For example, the 0D/3D composite reported in Nature
Communications (2024, 15: 4807) clearly illustrates this phenomenon:

However, the observation of well-defined ordering in 2D/2D heterostructures
remains a well-known and intrinsicchallenge, not specific to our system. In our study,
both PNs and BS possess characteristic 2D features and exhibit comparable lateral
dimensions. The inherently limited morphological contrast between the two
components makes it intrinsically difficult to resolve ordered interfaces at the
nanoscale. More importantly, physical perturbations during material preparation
further compromise structural ordering. For instance, the ultrasonic exfoliation
process for PNs production inevitably leads to fragmentation and edge irregularities;
and during the assembly of PNs and BS, random stacking orientations—such as
displacement, twisting, and slight curling of nanosheets—are essentially unavoidable.
These factors collectively diminish the likelihood of obtaining a well-ordered
compositestructure.
Recently, we have extensively surveyed the literature, including numerous
representative studies on 2D/2D heterojunctions. It is found that similar structural
features are widely reported across the field: even in seminal works, electron
microscopy images typically show coexisting nanosheets without consistent stacking
orientations and rarely display pronounced long-range ordering. For example, the
2D/2D composite reported in Journal of the American Chemical Society (2017, 139:
13234-13242) illustrates nanosheets with irregular orientations and no apparent
long-range order:

Hence, we believe our structural characterizations are consistent with what can

Nonetheless, this comment prompts us to further strengthen our experimental
evidence. We have added SEM images to characterize the morphology of each
components individually, clearly demonstrating that both PNs and BS exhibit
well-defined 2D structures in their monomeric states, particularly with identifiable
ordering. While, as discussed above, the ordered nature of the final 2D/2D composite
cannot be guaranteed, this does not detract from the key claim of our paper that “PNs

perspective” is examined in terms of what thermodynamic point of view and

Response: We thank the reviewer for the comment. From a thermodynamic
perspective, the generation of ROS during photocatalysis is governed by the redox
potentials of the relevant reactions relative to the semiconductor’s conduction and
valence band edges. If the conduction band minimum or valence band maximum of
the photocatalyst does not possess sufficient potential to drive the desired redox
reactions, the formation of ROS is thermodynamically limited, leading to energy loss.
As you noted, the relevant thermodynamic parameters essentially correspond to
whether the semiconductor’s conduction and valence band edges are sufficiently
positioned to drive the desired redox reactions. In response, we have supplemented

42.What does theaccumulation oflines in Figure2.(e),(f) indicate?
Response: Thanks for the comment. The data of Figure 2e and f can probe the
ultrafast dynamics of photo-excited charge carriers in 0.8PNs/BS system. By
monitoring ΔA over timescales from 0.5 ps to 3 ns, this technique allows us to
distinguish different processes: early-time positive signals reflect excited-state
absorption and carrier generation, while later-time negative signals correspond to
ground-state bleaching and stimulated emission, revealing carrier relaxation and
recombination. Importantly, the comparison between 0.0PNs/BS and 0.8PNs/BS
demonstrates enhanced stimulated emission in the latter, indicating more efficient
charge transfer across the heterojunction. Therefore, these data provide direct
evidence of how the heterojunction affects charge separation and recombination
dynamics, which is crucial for understanding and optimizingphotocatalyticactivity.

recombining radiatively. The connection arises because faster carrier separation

52.Does thetype ofBS affect planS-scheme?
Response: Thanks for the comment. The construction of an S-scheme
heterojunction mainly relies on two prerequisites: (i) the two semiconductors should
possess appropriate band structures to achieve staggered alignment, and (ii) there
should be a sufficiently large Fermi level difference to drive the internal electric field
for directional charge transfer (Chem, 2020, 6, 1543-1559). These two aspects are the
decisive factors for establishing an S-scheme charge transfer pathway. Whether BS is
p-type or n-type does not play the primary role. In practice, even n-n or p-p
combinations can form an effective S-scheme charge transfer pathway, provided the
above two conditions are met.Therefore, the type of BS is not the dominant factor; its
band edge positionsandFermi level alignment with PNsare thekey determinants.

58. What is your reason for writing this sentence “In this band alignment, PNs,
characterized by a more negative conduction-band position, act as the reduction-type
component, while BS, with a more positive valence-band position, function as the
oxidation-type component”.
Response: Thanks for the comment. The terminology of “reduction-type
component” and “oxidation-type component” reflects the distinct energetic positions
of the two semiconductors and the functional roles of their surviving charge carriers
under illumination. Specifically, PNs possess a more negative conduction-band
position, so the photo-excited electrons that remain in the conduction band after
interfacial recombination exhibit strong reduction potential. Conversely, BS have a
more positive valence-band position, and the photo-induced holes preserved in its
valence band show strong oxidation capability. This reduction–oxidation
complementarity is central to the S-scheme mechanism: the internal electric field
drives the recombination of low-energy carriers (electrons in BS and holes in PNs),
while selectively retaining the high-energy electrons in PNs and high-energy holes in
BS. As a result, the heterostructure maximizes the utilization of the intrinsic strong
redox potentials of the two components. The rationale for writing the sentence you
mentioned is now directly connected to the subsequent explanation in our manuscript.
Pleasesee pages 13-14 lines 258-266 in therevised manuscript as follows:
In the absence of light irradiation, electrons spontaneously transfer from PNs to BS,
establishing an internal electric field across the heterojunction directed from PNs to
BS. Under light irradiation, this built-in field facilitates the recombination of
photo-excited electrons in the conduction band of BS with photo-induced holes in the
valence band of PNs. Consequently, energetically favorable charge carriers are
preserved in the conduction band of PNs and the valence band of BS. Such an
S-scheme band alignment is anticipated to augment the ROS-production abilities of
charge carriers, effectively mitigating photon energy loss from a thermodynamic
perspective.
59.Are synthesized samples reusable (Recycling performance)? Please Perform XRD
analysis even after recovery (reuse).
Response: Thanks for the comment. We would like to emphasize an important
consideration regarding the evaluation of catalyst reusability. While many previous
studies, including some of our own prior works, relay on repeated batch experiments
to assess material recyclability, this approach has inherent limitations. Firstly, the
separation of photocatalyst powders from bacterial cells or bacterial residues is
technically challenging and often incomplete, which can lead to misleading
conclusions about material stability. Secondly,during repeated use,inevitable material
loss may occur, leading to a decrease in the actual recovery yield and affecting the
accuracy of performance evaluation. More importantly, powdered photocatalysts are
primarily research tools used to elucidate fundamental mechanisms, but are not
practical for real-world water disinfection applications. Therefore, evaluating material
stabilitysolely based onrepeated batch recycling tests lacks practical relevance.
To address this, we have pioneered the incorporation of our catalyst into a
continuous-flow fixed-bed reactor, enabling the direct assessment of disinfection
performance stability over extended operation (Advanced Materials. 2025, 37,
2410221). In the current work, our results demonstrate that after 24 h of continuous
operation, the disinfection efficiency remains above 99.99%, confirming the excellent
reusability ofthecatalyst ina realisticapplication setting.

27. In comment 33, do other parameters such as solvent viscosity and polarity also
have an effect?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. Indeed, other solvent
parameters can also influence the exfoliation process. Taking polarity, as you
mentioned, as an example, it can affect the interactions between 2D materials and
exfoliating mediums. As described in Science, 2011, 331: 568-571, the Hansen
solubility parameters provide an approach to quantify how exfoliating medium
influences the exfoliation process. These parameters incorporate three contributions to
the cohesive energy density: dispersion, polar, and hydrogen-bonding interactions. In
practice, effective exfoliation of a specific 2D material can only be achieved when all
three parameters (dispersion, polar, and hydrogen bond) of the solvent closely match
those of the 2D material. As can be seen, polarity is not an independent parameter,
rather, it is inherently embedded within the Hansen parameter set. That is to say,
although polarity is one of the parameters influencing exfoliation, its effect cannot be
clearly isolated from other intermolecular interactions, making it methodologically
challenging to use polarity as an independent screening criterion. In other words,
while polarity does play a role, it is not appropriate to treat it as a standalone indicator
for solvent selection.
In contrast, the surface energy is an independent parameter that has been widely
and successfully used for initial solvent selection. Although other parameters may
influence the exfoliation process, their existence does not undermine the validity of
using surface energy as a reliable descriptor, which is well supported by the
experimental results in this work. Also, many classical studies have employed surface
energy as a guiding parameter to identify suitable exfoliating mediums for various 2D
materials (J. Am. Chem. Soc, 2013, 135: 18-21; ACS Nano, 2016, 10: 2745-2751; Nat.
Nanotechnol, 2008, 3: 563-568). We hope that this clarification addresses your
concern.

For semiconductor heterojunctions, the key photophysical processes following
light excitation include excited-state absorption, ground-state bleaching, and
stimulated emission. It is worth noting that while all these processes can occur, they
evolve on different time scales. To facilitate understanding, we give an example: upon
light excitation, a molecule can undergo numerous distinct photophysical processes
(such as fluorescence, phosphorescence, internal conversion, and so on), as depicted
in the following schematic:
23
[Figure Redacted]
All these processes may take place within a photo-excited system, but their
characteristic lifetimes differ by several orders of magnitude, ranging from fs-s, as
shown below:
[Figure Redacted]
Similarly, after light excitation, in semiconductor heterojunctions, processes such
as excited-state absorption, ground-state bleaching, and stimulated emission also take
place on different time scales. To investigate these ultrafast photophysical processes,
femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy, conducted in our study, is a
powerful technique, as it allows direct tracking of the dynamic evolution of
these processes. The configuration of a femtosecond transient absorption
spectrometer is illustrated as follows:
[Figure Redacted]
In the above figure, the light emitted from the green instrument is used to excite
the sample, and after a very short delay (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......), a probe beam (from the
blue instrument) monitors the changes in the sample’s absorption. Femtosecond
transient absorption spectroscopy can be understood as an “ultrafast version” of
UV-vis absorption spectroscopy, recording the evolution of the sample’s absorption
over time with femtosecond time resolution. However, when directly comparing
absorption spectra at, for example, 0.0 ps and 0.5 ps, it is difficult to visually discern
significant differences, as the changes are typically very small. To facilitate
observation, the data in femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy are plotted
using ΔA on the vertical axis, where ΔA = A − A , representing the difference
excited ground
between the excited-state and ground-state absorption. The sign of ΔA can be used to
identify which photophysical process dominates at a given timescale. For instance,
when ΔA < 0, this indicates the occurrence of ground-state bleaching. This is because
that, before excitation, most electrons in the semiconductor material reside in the
ground state. Upon light excitation, some of these electrons are promoted to the
excited state, reducing the population of ground-state electrons—that is, fewer
electrons are available to absorb the probe beam (from the blue instrument). As a
result, the measured absorption signal decreases, manifesting as a negative ΔA.
In summary, based on the detailed explanation above, we hope it is now clear
what the curves in Figures 2e and f represent: each curve corresponds to the
absorption change between the excited-state and ground-state sample (0.0PNs/BS or
0.8PNs/BS) at a specific delay time (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......). Plotting the curves measured
at different delay times on one figure is simply a way to visually illustrate the spectral
evolution over time (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......), and does not imply any “accumulation” of
the signal. We hope this explanation makes it clear.

The authors have attempted to optimize the compatibility between the macroscopic geometric and microscopic band structures of the heterojunction components to address the kinetic and thermodynamic limitations of photo-induced charge carriers. Response: In response to the reviewer’s comment on the absence of a
well-ordered structure in the TEM images, we provide the following clarification.
Indeed, electron microscopy images of many heterojunction systems often reveal a
certain degree of ordering, particularly in 0D/2D or 0D/3D composite materials. This
is largely attributable to the small size and distinct morphological feature of the 0D
components, which offer strong contrast and clear geometric distinction when
dispersed on 2D or 3D substrates.As a result, such composites tend to exhibit visually
recognizable ordering. For example, the 0D/3D composite reported in Nature
Communications (2024, 15: 4807) clearly illustrates this phenomenon:
[Figure Redacted]
FigureR1.ElectronmicroscopyimagesofIn O /Nb O heterojunctionillustratingthedeposition

of0Dmaterialsontoa3Dsubstrate.
However, the observation of well-defined ordering in 2D/2D heterostructures
remains a well-known and intrinsicchallenge, not specific to our system. In our study,
both PNs and BS possess characteristic 2D features and exhibit comparable lateral
dimensions. The inherently limited morphological contrast between the two
components makes it intrinsically difficult to resolve ordered interfaces at the
nanoscale. More importantly, physical perturbations during material preparation
further compromise structural ordering. For instance, the ultrasonic exfoliation
process for PNs production inevitably leads to fragmentation and edge irregularities;
and during the assembly of PNs and BS, random stacking orientations—such as
displacement, twisting, and slight curling of nanosheets—are essentially unavoidable.
These factors collectively diminish the likelihood of obtaining a well-ordered
compositestructure.
Recently, we have extensively surveyed the literature, including numerous
representative studies on 2D/2D heterojunctions. It is found that similar structural
features are widely reported across the field: even in seminal works, electron
microscopy images typically show coexisting nanosheets without consistent stacking
orientations and rarely display pronounced long-range ordering. For example, the
2D/2D composite reported in Journal of the American Chemical Society (2017, 139:
13234-13242) illustrates nanosheets with irregular orientations and no apparent
long-range order:

19.Whydid you chooseBiOI- BiOBr or BiOCl?
Response: Thanks for the comment. We chose BiOI, BiOBr, and BiOCl because
our study aims to demonstrate that optimizing the compatibility between the
macroscopic geometric structures of heterojunction components can effectively
overcome the kinetic constraint in photo-induced charge carrier. PNs have a typical
2D structure, and all members of the BiOX (X = I, Br, Cl) family likewise crystallize
in2D layered structures, making themsuitable candidates to probethis concept.
The core of this work is to investigate 2D/2D heterojunctions (composed of BS
and PNs) to demonstrate the underlying scientific hypothesis. To further validate the
hypothesis, it is desirable to examine other 2D/2D materials. However, if the second
2D component differs too much in intrinsic properties—such as using carbon nitride
with very different band structure and surface chemistry—the results could be
dominated by these property mismatches, making it difficult to isolate the effect of
2D/2D structural compatibility itself. In contrast, selecting chemically and structurally
similar materials like BiOBr or BiOCl preserves comparable electronic and surface
characteristics while maintaining the 2D morphology. This allows a more direct and
convincing demonstration that the observed enhancements arise from geometric and
interfacial compatibility, rather than other confounding material differences. For the

52.Does thetype ofBS affect planS-scheme?
Response: Thanks for the comment. The construction of an S-scheme
heterojunction mainly relies on two prerequisites: (i) the two semiconductors should
possess appropriate band structures to achieve staggered alignment, and (ii) there
should be a sufficiently large Fermi level difference to drive the internal electric field
for directional charge transfer (Chem, 2020, 6, 1543-1559). These two aspects are the
decisive factors for establishing an S-scheme charge transfer pathway. Whether BS is
p-type or n-type does not play the primary role. In practice, even n-n or p-p
combinations can form an effective S-scheme charge transfer pathway, provided the
above two conditions are met.Therefore, the type of BS is not the dominant factor; its
band edge positionsandFermi level alignment with PNsare thekey determinants.

57.Does PNs have an absorption edge in UV-visdiffusereflectance spectroscopy?
Response: Thanks for the comment. In principle, PNs should exhibit an
absorption edge. However, obtaining such data through UV-vis diffuse reflectance
spectroscopy is challenging. This is because few-layer PNs can only be stably
maintained in a dispersed liquid phase. Once removed from the liquid
environment—as required for UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectroscopy measurements

feature becomes indistinct or absent in the UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectroscopy
results. To address this, we performed UV-vis absorbance spectroscopy on PNs

58. What is your reason for writing this sentence “In this band alignment, PNs,
characterized by a more negative conduction-band position, act as the reduction-type
component, while BS, with a more positive valence-band position, function as the
oxidation-type component”.
Response: Thanks for the comment. The terminology of “reduction-type
component” and “oxidation-type component” reflects the distinct energetic positions
of the two semiconductors and the functional roles of their surviving charge carriers
under illumination. Specifically, PNs possess a more negative conduction-band
position, so the photo-excited electrons that remain in the conduction band after
interfacial recombination exhibit strong reduction potential. Conversely, BS have a
more positive valence-band position, and the photo-induced holes preserved in its
valence band show strong oxidation capability. This reduction–oxidation
complementarity is central to the S-scheme mechanism: the internal electric field
drives the recombination of low-energy carriers (electrons in BS and holes in PNs),
while selectively retaining the high-energy electrons in PNs and high-energy holes in
BS. As a result, the heterostructure maximizes the utilization of the intrinsic strong
redox potentials of the two components. The rationale for writing the sentence you
mentioned is now directly connected to the subsequent explanation in our manuscript.
Pleasesee pages 13-14 lines 258-266 in therevised manuscript as follows:
In the absence of light irradiation, electrons spontaneously transfer from PNs to BS,
establishing an internal electric field across the heterojunction directed from PNs to
BS. Under light irradiation, this built-in field facilitates the recombination of
photo-excited electrons in the conduction band of BS with photo-induced holes in the
valence band of PNs. Consequently, energetically favorable charge carriers are
preserved in the conduction band of PNs and the valence band of BS. Such an
S-scheme band alignment is anticipated to augment the ROS-production abilities of
charge carriers, effectively mitigating photon energy loss from a thermodynamic
perspective.
59.Are synthesized samples reusable (Recycling performance)? Please Perform XRD
analysis even after recovery (reuse).
Response: Thanks for the comment. We would like to emphasize an important
consideration regarding the evaluation of catalyst reusability. While many previous
studies, including some of our own prior works, relay on repeated batch experiments
to assess material recyclability, this approach has inherent limitations. Firstly, the
separation of photocatalyst powders from bacterial cells or bacterial residues is
technically challenging and often incomplete, which can lead to misleading
conclusions about material stability. Secondly,during repeated use,inevitable material
loss may occur, leading to a decrease in the actual recovery yield and affecting the
accuracy of performance evaluation. More importantly, powdered photocatalysts are
primarily research tools used to elucidate fundamental mechanisms, but are not
practical for real-world water disinfection applications. Therefore, evaluating material
stabilitysolely based onrepeated batch recycling tests lacks practical relevance.
To address this, we have pioneered the incorporation of our catalyst into a
continuous-flow fixed-bed reactor, enabling the direct assessment of disinfection
performance stability over extended operation (Advanced Materials. 2025, 37,
2410221). In the current work, our results demonstrate that after 24 h of continuous
operation, the disinfection efficiency remains above 99.99%, confirming the excellent
reusability ofthecatalyst ina realisticapplication setting.

In this figure, the band structure of a typical S-scheme heterojunction is depicted.

consistent with previously reported studies (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. Engl, 2020, 59:
5218-5225; Chem, 2020, 6: 1543-1559). We hope this explanation addresses your

27. In comment 33, do other parameters such as solvent viscosity and polarity also
have an effect?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. Indeed, other solvent
parameters can also influence the exfoliation process. Taking polarity, as you
mentioned, as an example, it can affect the interactions between 2D materials and
exfoliating mediums. As described in Science, 2011, 331: 568-571, the Hansen
solubility parameters provide an approach to quantify how exfoliating medium
influences the exfoliation process. These parameters incorporate three contributions to
the cohesive energy density: dispersion, polar, and hydrogen-bonding interactions. In
practice, effective exfoliation of a specific 2D material can only be achieved when all
three parameters (dispersion, polar, and hydrogen bond) of the solvent closely match
those of the 2D material. As can be seen, polarity is not an independent parameter,
rather, it is inherently embedded within the Hansen parameter set. That is to say,
although polarity is one of the parameters influencing exfoliation, its effect cannot be
clearly isolated from other intermolecular interactions, making it methodologically
challenging to use polarity as an independent screening criterion. In other words,
while polarity does play a role, it is not appropriate to treat it as a standalone indicator
for solvent selection.
In contrast, the surface energy is an independent parameter that has been widely
and successfully used for initial solvent selection. Although other parameters may
influence the exfoliation process, their existence does not undermine the validity of
using surface energy as a reliable descriptor, which is well supported by the
experimental results in this work. Also, many classical studies have employed surface
energy as a guiding parameter to identify suitable exfoliating mediums for various 2D
materials (J. Am. Chem. Soc, 2013, 135: 18-21; ACS Nano, 2016, 10: 2745-2751; Nat.
Nanotechnol, 2008, 3: 563-568). We hope that this clarification addresses your
concern.

28. In comment 42, Explain accumulation of lines further. What does it represent?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. In our previous response, we
may have provided an overly brief explanation. In this round, we offer a more detailed
clarification regarding your question: “Explain accumulation of lines further. What
does it represent?” In short: “Each curve in Figures 2e and f represents the absorption
change between the excited and ground states of the material (0.0PNs/BS or
0.8PNs/BS) at a specific delay time (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......), and plotting multiple curves
on one figure simply visualizes the spectral evolution over time without implying any
“accumulation” of the signal. A more detailed explanation is provided below.
For semiconductor heterojunctions, the key photophysical processes following
light excitation include excited-state absorption, ground-state bleaching, and
stimulated emission. It is worth noting that while all these processes can occur, they
evolve on different time scales. To facilitate understanding, we give an example: upon
light excitation, a molecule can undergo numerous distinct photophysical processes
(such as fluorescence, phosphorescence, internal conversion, and so on), as depicted
in the following schematic:
23
[Figure Redacted]
All these processes may take place within a photo-excited system, but their
characteristic lifetimes differ by several orders of magnitude, ranging from fs-s, as
shown below:
[Figure Redacted]
Similarly, after light excitation, in semiconductor heterojunctions, processes such
as excited-state absorption, ground-state bleaching, and stimulated emission also take
place on different time scales. To investigate these ultrafast photophysical processes,
femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy, conducted in our study, is a
powerful technique, as it allows direct tracking of the dynamic evolution of
these processes. The configuration of a femtosecond transient absorption
spectrometer is illustrated as follows:
[Figure Redacted]
In the above figure, the light emitted from the green instrument is used to excite
the sample, and after a very short delay (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......), a probe beam (from the
blue instrument) monitors the changes in the sample’s absorption. Femtosecond
transient absorption spectroscopy can be understood as an “ultrafast version” of
UV-vis absorption spectroscopy, recording the evolution of the sample’s absorption
over time with femtosecond time resolution. However, when directly comparing
absorption spectra at, for example, 0.0 ps and 0.5 ps, it is difficult to visually discern
significant differences, as the changes are typically very small. To facilitate
observation, the data in femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy are plotted
using ΔA on the vertical axis, where ΔA = A − A , representing the difference
excited ground
between the excited-state and ground-state absorption. The sign of ΔA can be used to
identify which photophysical process dominates at a given timescale. For instance,
when ΔA < 0, this indicates the occurrence of ground-state bleaching. This is because
that, before excitation, most electrons in the semiconductor material reside in the
ground state. Upon light excitation, some of these electrons are promoted to the
excited state, reducing the population of ground-state electrons—that is, fewer
electrons are available to absorb the probe beam (from the blue instrument). As a
result, the measured absorption signal decreases, manifesting as a negative ΔA.
In summary, based on the detailed explanation above, we hope it is now clear
what the curves in Figures 2e and f represent: each curve corresponds to the
absorption change between the excited-state and ground-state sample (0.0PNs/BS or
0.8PNs/BS) at a specific delay time (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......). Plotting the curves measured
at different delay times on one figure is simply a way to visually illustrate the spectral
evolution over time (0.5, 1, 5, 10 ps......), and does not imply any “accumulation” of
the signal. We hope this explanation makes it clear.
